# JusPrin 2 pricing: the mental model (working doc, 2026-10-29)

Untracked working document for the pricing brainstorm. Facts, hypotheses, goal and comparables, kept apart on purpose. No recommendations here. Companion data: `v1-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (JusPrin v1 production data) and `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (Obico Pro production data, same audience).

Sourcing rule for the comparables: every figure comes from a page fetched or a search result read on 2026-10-29 by a research agent. "Vendor" marks a company's own page; "3P, loosely held" marks a third-party tracker, blog or news summary. Items from the original case list that no source supported are struck and listed at the end.

## Goal (Kenneth's words)

Traction, measured as active users and time in the app. Become the default AI harness for 3D slicing. Reduce friction as long as no choice now blocks turning profitable later. Collect feedback good enough to fine-tune small models later; willing to subsidise model cost to get it. The two audiences (people who already slice in OrcaSlicer, people who cannot) are believed to overlap heavily and converge. Sign-in is not required when the person uses their own API key.

Not yet decided: the traction number and horizon.

## Facts

### From JusPrin v1 production data (two years, read-only)

- 6,695 people, 31,566 chats, 34 payers ever, 20 paying now. Conversion since the paywall: 0.7%.
- Free active users: median 2 chats a month, 90th percentile 6. 41% of all users ever had exactly one chat.
- Payers: median 6.5 chats per 30 paid days, 90th percentile 51, max 130. First paid month median 17.5 chats; later months median 0. 64% of later paid months have no chats.
- Usage comes in project sessions: the busiest 7 days hold 80% of a typical month's chats, on about 4 distinct days. Weekend share 33%.
- 159 people ever hit the 50-call free cap; 14% of them subscribed. 25 of 41 subscriptions started within 30 days of hitting it. 1.1% of active free months reach the cap.
- 14 of 23 monthly subscriptions ended as failed renewal payments, often while the person was still active. One person re-subscribed 8 times.
- Explicit feedback: 14 ratings and 2 comments in 31,566 chats, from a rating control that was never inside the slicer. 40% of settings proposals got a typed follow-up; in a 60-message hand-coded sample about 1 in 6 corrected the agent or reported a print result, a third named a specific setting.
- Follow-ups are dominated by Portuguese and Spanish. Country mix not yet measured.
- Prices never changed ($6.99 monthly, $59.99 annual); no trials; no price-sensitivity data exists.
- Reading these numbers (Kenneth, 2026-10-29): the low medians measure low stickiness, not what an engaged person does with the product. 41% of users had one chat and 64% of later paid months were empty because people stopped using v1, so a median over all of them describes churn. The nearest measure of an engaged month is the first paid month: median 17.5 chats and 29 model calls (20.8 chats for annual subscribers), with the per-30-day 90th percentile at 51 chats.

### From Obico Pro production data (same audience, 2019 to 2026, read-only; `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md`)

- 251,073 signups, 12,488 ever paid: lifetime conversion is 5.0% (Kenneth's recollection of about 5% matches). Everyone gets an automatic 30-day Pro trial with no card. Of the people who did pay, 47% paid within 35 days of signup and 24% in days 25 to 35, so the trial's end is the moment most payers convert. That 47% is a share of payers, not a conversion rate.
- Obico already runs a rewarded feedback programme: the app asks the person to label a print frame ("It contains spaghetti" / "It does NOT contain spaghetti", `PrintShotFeedback`) and credits detection hours for answering. Kenneth's experience: the labels are high quality, not gamed. This is the closest evidence on rewarded feedback for this audience. The enterprise admin keeps a per-label human review flag (`PrintShotFeedbackReview.invalid` in `tsd-enterprise/web_ent/app_ent/models.py`), so the share of bad labels is countable from the database; not yet counted. The crediting code is in the open-source server, which is not checked out on this machine.
- Conversion within a year of signup fell from 6 to 9% (2019 to 2022 cohorts) to 4.0% (2023), 2.1% (2024), 1.5% (2025). Signups did not fall. The cause is unknown from this data.
- Price rose twice: $3/$4.50 at launch (annual-per-month / monthly) in 2019, $4/$6 from 2020, $6.99/$8.99 from May 2026 with existing subscribers moved to $5.49/$7.49 loyalty plans unless they opted out. Only 22 legacy-priced subscriptions remain, so almost nobody opted out.
- Annual is 58% of first subscriptions. 77% of annual subscriptions renew at the first anniversary (70 to 80% by cohort); 57% are still paid at two years. Monthly: 82% survive the first renewal, 35% are paying at one year, 19% at two.
- 30% of cancellations are failed payments, 70% cancel clicks (v1 monthly: 14 of 18 were failed payments). Typed cancel reasons by keyword bucket: not printing enough or not using it 4,085; detection quality 1,696; price or cost 1,237; printer sold or broken 350.
- Usage after subscribing decays with the same shape as v1 but less steeply: mean prints 53.6 in the first paid month, 34.4 in the second, 13.9 in the twelfth; 40% of paid months 2 to 12 have zero prints (v1: 64% of later paid months have zero chats). People subscribe during a busy printing stretch (first month is 25% above the month before). Annual renewals hold at 77% despite half of month-12 subscribers printing nothing that month.
- Country, by card-issuing country: Obico card payers 64% US; JusPrin v1 payers 16 of 34 Brazilian, 5 US. By mobile-app timezone: Obico payers 58% US; JusPrin v1 chat users 35% US, 10% Brazil, 7.5% Germany. 10 of v1's 15 failed renewals were Brazilian cards. Only 2.9% of v1 chat users ever paid for Obico Pro.
- Decline reasons are generic: "card declined" and "insufficient funds" dominate in both products; Chargebee does not record whether a cross-border or recurring charge was refused.

### From the current system

- JusPrin Cloud is live. The gateway routes per user and per request with a server-side assignment by user hash, so routing or price A/B is mechanically possible.
- Bring-your-own-key exists for Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter.
- Obico billing already has subscriptions, trials and a metered credit unit.
- A DeepSeek-class model has run in the harness; the pinned hosts could not take images.

### From other businesses (verified 2026-10-29)

**Caps, "unlimited" and what happens at the limit**

- ChatGPT Free is limited to "a limited number of times within a five hour window" with no number on the help page (vendor, help article via snippet). Numbers (Free 10 per 5 h, Plus 160 per 3 h, then fallback to a mini model inside the same chat) exist only in third-party summaries (3P, loosely held). Complaint threads are about silent routing to a smaller model, not about the count. The August 2025 GPT-5 launch spike had Plus raised from 80 to 160 per 3 h within days (3P).
- Midjourney: Relax mode "is unlimited" and only slower; unused Fast time "doesn't carry over" (vendor docs via snippet). Anchoring on hours is visible in user writing ("I usually run out of fast hours around the 25th", 2024). Relax is possible because idle GPU queue time has near-zero marginal cost.
- Windsurf: the "unlimited in-house model" premise is partly stale. SWE-1-lite was "available for unlimited use to all users" at launch (vendor, 2025-05-15); today's page sells a "usage allowance" that "refreshes automatically on a daily and weekly basis" and says "Most users will never hit their limits" (vendor, undated). Kilo Code: no in-house model exists; it passes through provider rates with no markup (vendor).
- Claude Pro: "at least 5x more usage per 5-hour session than Free", "Usage limits apply", no number (vendor). Users surprised by a weekly limit on top of the 5-hour one (Reddit, 2026-02).
- Perplexity Pro: "access may be limited during weeks of especially heavy usage", no number (vendor). A May 2026 Reddit wave when people were cut to Basic while the meter showed searches left.
- Gemini: "compute-based usage limits", refresh "every 5 hours until you reach your weekly limit", subscribers at the limit "can keep chatting with Flash-Lite" (vendor help).
- Adobe Firefly: credits announced 2023 as "may not" be enforced; enforcement began 2025; the 2024 promise of "slower after credits" became a hard paywall; Pro repriced $59.99 to $69.99 with "unlimited standard" generation plus metered premium credits (3P quoting Adobe; vendor plans page confirms "unlimited standard image and vector generations"). Forum anger was about unexplained deductions and surprise walls.

**Free tiers that cost real money per use**

- Meshy: 100 free credits a month, a generation is 20 credits; monthly credits do not roll over, purchased ones do not expire; free users cannot download current-generation output (vendor docs). The free allowance changed three times in August 2026 (3P tracker, loosely held). Company-reported $100M ARR (unaudited, 2026-09).
- Tripo: 200 free credits a month "≈ 13 Models" (vendor via snippet); a reviewer finds best-quality generations cost 55 credits, so 3 to 4 models in practice.
- Rodin (Hyper3D): "pay only when you confirm results": generation is free, credits are spent on download; Creator $30 a month (vendor).
- Suno: Free "50 credits per day", "No monthly song downloads", 7 lifetime downloads since 2026-09; Pro $8 a month billed yearly with 2,500 credits; credits do not carry over (vendor). Udio: similar daily allowance (3P only; official page returned nothing).
- Canva Free: "up to 200 uses of Standard AI or up to 20 uses of Premium AI" a month, cheap tools uncounted, meter visible under billing (vendor via snippet; 3P). CapCut: free AI caps framed as "a limited-time free trial offered during the Beta phase" (vendor help).
- Struck: "$8 to 20 entry plans" for 3D generation tools. None in the set is under $20; Rodin is $30.

**Open-source harness plus optional hosted convenience**

- Home Assistant / Nabu Casa: $6.50 a month or $65 a year, 31-day trial, no card; the pricing page lists "Funds the development of Home Assistant" as a benefit and says "Your purchases alone fund our work"; "Home Assistant works fully without it" (vendor, fetched). Launched at $5 in 2018: "Relying on donations makes budgeting for employees impossible." No subscriber count published anywhere. Users say they pay to support the project and to avoid maintaining free alternatives.
- Zed: free "Unlimited use with your API keys"; Pro went from $20 with 500 prompts to $10 with $5 of tokens, overage at API list price +10% (vendor, 2025-09-24), because "LLM bills have become our biggest expense, and more paying customers translates to more money lost". HN: "little value in subscribing to Zed Pro compared to just bringing my own API key".
- Cline: "Model Inference at Cost or BYOK"; no individual paid plan on the official page (vendor).
- Roo Code and Continue: struck as live cases. Roo Code shut its extension, Cloud and Router on 2026-05-15 and pivoted; Continue joined Cursor and shut its hub in 2026-07 (3P news).
- Ollama: local use "always unlimited"; cloud pay-per-token or $20 a month with $60 credits (vendor). Open WebUI: no hosted or individual paid plan (vendor).

**What a paid plan sells in hobbyist markets; failed payments**

- MakerWorld, Printables, Thangs: no platform charges hobbyists for access. Every paid layer is creator-run (commercial licences, clubs, per-designer memberships, a $14.99 download bundle at Thangs) and the free catalogue is explicitly protected (vendor blogs). Printables' store has a $5 minimum price.
- Strava: "$6.67/month" billed yearly at $79.99, "Save 44%"; several plans annual only (vendor). Its 2023 price rise drew cancel threats and an admission it had failed to tell monthly payers that switching to annual avoided the increase.
- onX Hunt: annual as "Best Value"; on lapse the person's own saved markups stay free (vendor). Planta: annual emphasised at a large discount (App Store listing; 3P).
- Dunning: Stripe claims recovery tools "recover 56% of failed recurring payments on average" (vendor marketing, loosely held); a competitor puts B2C Stripe accounts at 25 to 35% (3P). Chargebee: "80-90% of the transactions are soft declines"; "20–40% of all customer churn is payment-failure-led" (vendor, citing others). Peloton attributed about half of a churn increase to the timing of post-failure emails (3P, 2026-08).

**Brazil and Latin America**

- Entry tiers of global brands in Brazil run at roughly 22 to 54% of the US price at the 2026-10-28 central-bank rate of R$5.342: Spotify R$23.90 vs $12.99 (34%), YouTube Premium R$26.90 vs $15.99 (31%), Netflix with ads R$25.90 vs $8.99 (54%), Super Duolingo R$14.99 vs about $9.99 to 12.99 (22 to 28%) (vendor pages and press, Oct 2026).
- ChatGPT Go launched in Brazil on 2025-10-28 at R$39.99 a month, about $7.49, "65% cheaper than Plus", with all plans switched to BRL billing to remove "oscilação cambial e IOF", and a Nubank distribution deal giving 1 to 12 free months (Nubank newsroom; press). India and Indonesia launched earlier at about $4.50. OpenAI said India paid subscribers "more than doubled" in Go's first month (3P quoting OpenAI).
- Spotify takes Pix as prepaid blocks only (no auto-renew); Netflix takes no Pix at checkout (vendor newsroom; 3P). Pix Automático (recurring Pix) has been live since June 2025.
- Cross-border USD card charges hit three failure modes: cards not enabled for international use by default, FX fraud scoring, FX spending caps (dLocal, PagBrasil; vendor guides). Every approval-uplift number found is payment-vendor marketing.
- Stripe lets US-domiciled merchants accept Pix from Brazilian customers, presented in BRL and settled in USD, including recurring charges through Pix Automático; a 3.5% IOF tax line is added to the customer by default, recurring charges carry a 3-day pre-debit notice, and the statement shows Ebanx rather than the merchant (vendor docs, live). Chargebee's Pix-via-Stripe is private beta, BRL only, CPF/CNPJ mandatory. Boleto via Stripe does need a Brazil-based Stripe account. BRL pricing in Chargebee needs a cloned plan per currency. An earlier claim that Pix needs a Brazilian entity was wrong; the reverse holds for Pix Automático.

**Feedback incentives and own-model swaps**

- Midjourney rating parties offer no reward; the page calls rating junk "a very important part of our process" (vendor, 2025-03-30). A separate daily rating queue gives the top 2,000 raters one Fast hour (vendor help via snippet). Struck: rating parties paying Fast hours.
- Tesla FSD Beta gated access on a Safety Score, then required consent to vehicle-linked video after safety events (press, 2021). Testers said openly they were gaming the score.
- Common Voice goals: small, measured lifts in return rate; Mozilla called them "modest" and said nothing about quality (vendor forum, 2019). The Open Data Institute warns leaderboards incentivise volume "regardless of whether they are useful".
- Duolingo's Birdbrain learns from exercise outcomes alone, shadow-mode then A/B; no explicit rating step (press and vendor blog).
- Perplexity offered its own Sonar model to Pro as an optional default after A/B on satisfaction, price unchanged (vendor, 2025-02). Cursor retrained Tab on accept/reject behaviour, 28% higher accept rate, no pricing mention (vendor, 2025-09); its own Composer model was metered "the same as GPT-5" and drew complaints. Character.ai stopped training frontier models in 2024; the 2026 removal of old models drew "Terrible compared to the models you got rid of" (press). Struck: a dated own-model swap at Jasper or Grammarly; both describe a blend.

## Hypotheses

Each is a hypothesis until the named check is done. Survey evidence is noted where it bears on one.

1. **A premium chat costs $0.20 to $0.50 for a simple case.** Kenneth's estimate. Measured 2026-10-28 on Opus 5.5 in three harness chats: $0.30, $0.43 and $0.56. **Measured 2026-10-30 on Opus 5.5, pictures on, source at `2f9d322dee` (`journey-cost-2026-10.md`), one run each:** a simple 3-turn session $0.30, which fits, but a 5-turn troubleshooting session $0.64 ($0.66 with a photo) and a 6-turn complex session $1.27 do not. These are sessions with several turns and slices, so the range holds for the simple case only. Scripted turns follow within seconds; a person who pauses over 5 minutes before every turn would pay about $0.64, $2.56 and $1.49 (calculated from the logs, not measured), because Anthropic's cache lasts 5 minutes and rewriting it is the largest cost. **Measured 2026-11-01 on Claude Sonnet 5.5, pictures on, same scripted words, source `69780c7af4` plus the harness fix `01ec46a4af` (a newer build than the Opus runs; `journey-cost-2026-10.md`, "Sonnet 5.5, added 2026-11-01"), one run each:** the same sessions cost $0.19 (simple, 3 turns), $0.34 (complex, 6 turns) and $0.35 ($0.37 with the photo, troubleshooting, 5 turns), priced at Sonnet 5.5's rates of $2 input, $0.10 cache read, $2.50 five-minute cache write and $10 output per million tokens (fetched 2026-11-01). That is 0.64, 0.26 and 0.55 (0.56 with photo) of Opus's cost, and 0.40 over all 14 user messages ($0.063 a message against Opus's $0.158 and DeepSeek's $0.024). So the assumption that a Sonnet-class expert tier costs about half of Opus holds on two sessions (0.55 to 0.64, because Sonnet used 11 to 28% more tokens than Opus on the same words) and is pessimistic on the third (0.26, because Opus's complex run paid a $0.36 cache expiry during a slow slice and Sonnet's did not). The simple Sonnet session ($0.19) is just under the $0.20 to $0.50 range; the troubleshooting and complex sessions ($0.35, $0.34) fall inside it. Caveat: the Opus and Sonnet runs used different builds, and I did not run Opus on the new one. Check: gateway token accounting on real v2 chats, including real pauses.
2. **A cheap model costs roughly 15 to 30 times less per chat.** Guess from memory. **Measured 2026-10-30, same build, DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter with pictures removed, one run each:** $0.015, $0.31 and $0.020 against Opus's $0.30, $1.27 and $0.64, so 20 times, 4 times and 33 times less. The 4 times is the complex session, where DeepSeek polled the slicer 75 times during a slow slice on a debug build; those requests were two thirds of its cost, and without them the ratio is about 12 times (calculated). Answer quality was not compared. Check: gateway accounting on a shipped build, and whether the polling can be stopped.
3. **An engaged v2 user's monthly usage is unknown, and v1's overall medians do not estimate it.** Earlier versions of this model used v1's median payer (6.5 chats per 30 days) as "typical demand" and concluded a sub-$10 all-premium plan was profitable for most payers. That was wrong: the medians describe people who had stopped using v1. Using the first paid month instead (median 17.5 chats, 90th percentile 51 per 30 days) and Kenneth's $0.35 per chat, an engaged month costs about $6 at the median and $18 at the 90th percentile, so a $7 flat all-premium plan sits at break-even for the engaged median and underwater for the engaged tail. Kenneth's expectation (confirmed 2026-10-29): an engaged v2 user will use more than v1's first paid month showed, because v1's low numbers came from people leaving. So v1's first month is a floor for engaged usage, not an estimate, and v2 starts chats on file open and runs tools, which pushes the same way. Consequence: at $0.35 a chat an engaged user costs more than $6 a month on a frontier model, so a sub-$10 all-premium flat plan is underwater for engaged people from the start, and the cheap model or a budget is a launch question, not a later one. With the 2026-10-30 session measurements (Opus 5.5 $0.30 for a simple session, $0.64 for troubleshooting, $1.27 for a complex one, before real pauses), the same floor month costs $5 to $22 at the median of 17.5 sessions and $15 to $65 at the 90th percentile of 51, depending on the mix; on DeepSeek V4 Flash the same months cost $0.26 to $5.40 and $0.77 to $16, with the complex-session figure inflated by slice polling on a debug build. Check: beta cohort on the live gateway, measured on people still active in month two.
4. **The cheap model is good enough for the basic job.** Untested on the real task. Check: prompt eval harness vs Sonnet on print-setup cases, with image handling, at approved spend.
5. **A visible cap becomes a break-even anchor.** Supported in part: Midjourney users plan their month around hours. Refined by the survey: the anger spike in every case is at the boundary (silent swaps, meters disagreeing with cutoffs, "slower" turning into a wall), not at the number itself.
6. **A fallback keeps the session and still converts; a wall ends it.** ChatGPT and Gemini both degrade rather than stop, and the complaints are about the swap being silent. Unmeasured whether a fallback converts.
7. **Behaviour carries training signal for free, and rewarded explicit feedback from this audience is high quality.** The first half is supported by v1 (about 3,000 corrective follow-ups against 16 ratings) and by the surveyed cases that published measured gains (Duolingo, Cursor Tab). The second half comes from Obico's own rewarded print-shot labelling, which Kenneth reports produced good data. An earlier version of this hypothesis said rewards invite gaming; the survey did not support that. It found no evidence either way on Midjourney's rating data, one gamed gate at Tesla that was an access score rather than a reward for feedback, and a general warning from the Open Data Institute about leaderboards. That was one case and a caution, overstated into a pattern. Possible reasons Obico's result differs from the general worry, all untested: makers are a more conscientious population, and a small company's reward feels like a fair trade rather than something to exploit. The open question is no longer whether to reward feedback but what to ask, when, and how the reward relates to the missing label, "did the print work".
8. **The two audiences overlap and converge.** Kenneth's guess. Check: segment v1 users by whether they edit settings themselves.
9. **The July 2025 usage drop was launch decay, not the paywall.** My reading. Check: the July cohort's later behaviour.
10. **Grandfathering early payers is cheap.** True at tens of payers by arithmetic.
11. **The user base is heavily Brazilian; failed renewals are payment-method failures.** Half confirmed: v1 users are 35% US and 10% Brazil, but v1 payers are 16 of 34 Brazilian and 10 of 15 failed renewals were Brazilian cards. The payment-method mechanism is still unconfirmed: Chargebee records only "card declined" and "insufficient funds", never whether a cross-border or recurring charge was refused. Obico, 64% US payers, loses 30% of cancellations to failed payments too, so part of v1's rate is ordinary.
19. **New from Obico: a trial end converts more reliably than a usage cap.** Obico's lifetime conversion is 5%, and nearly half of its payers paid within the automatic trial window; v1 converted 0.7%, at a cap that 1% of months reach. Untested whether a trial works here: v1's median first week was 2.5 chats, but that median includes the 41% who never came back, so an engaged person's first week is unknown and almost certainly busier.
20. **New from Obico: the leading stated reason for cancelling is not using the product, far ahead of price.** This fits v1's silent later months. It is a hypothesis that a plan costing nothing in idle months (prepaid, usage-based, or annual priced for insurance) retains better than monthly; Obico's 77% annual renewal despite half-silent month 12 is the one data point.
21. **New from Obico: conversion in this audience fell four-fold after 2022 for unknown reasons**, while signups grew. Whatever caused it may bear on JusPrin's funnel too; nothing here tests the printer-camera explanation.
12. **New from the survey: "unlimited" survives only where marginal cost is near zero** (idle GPU queue, tab completions, own small models). No surveyed vendor offers unlimited frontier chat. For JusPrin this holds until the own-model phase.
13. **New: flat-fee hosted inference on rented frontier models gets repriced within about a year** (Zed) or the business leaves (Roo, Continue). Observed in daily-use professional tools with high token volume; a hobbyist slicer's volume is far lower, so the dynamic may not apply at the same scale.
14. **New: free tiers in costly-generation tools gate the artefact, not the generation** (download, export, commercial rights). A slicer chat has no equivalent artefact; the question is whether anything in JusPrin plays that role.
15. **New: a daily reset fits bursty hobby use better than a monthly one** (Suno). Untested here; v1 bursts are multi-day project sessions, not single days.
16. **New: "beta" or "trial" wording on a free allowance keeps the option to change it** (CapCut, Adobe's unenforced credits). Adobe shows the cost: the later enforcement was read as a bait and switch.
17. **New: seasonal hobby apps make annual the default and keep the person's own data free on lapse** (Strava, onX). v1's annual payers used about 33 chats a year against $59.99, a churn-shaped average (most of those years went quiet after the first month), not what an engaged year looks like.
18. **New: a quarter to half of failed renewals are recoverable by retries and email timing** (vendor figures). v1's 14 of 23 is too small a sample for a rate.

## Comparables: what transfers to a sub-$10 hobbyist slicer, and what does not

| Case | Transfers | Does not transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Obico Pro (own data, same audience) | Automatic no-card trial as the conversion moment (5% lifetime conversion, half of payers inside the trial window); annual at 58% of first subscriptions renewing at 77%; price rises absorbed via loyalty pricing; "not using it" as the top cancel reason; 30% involuntary churn as the baseline; rewarded print-shot labels that came back high quality | Monitoring is always-on insurance with near-zero marginal cost per idle month; Obico payers are 58 to 64% US while v1 payers were mostly Brazilian; only 2.9% overlap between the user bases |
| ChatGPT Free/Plus | Degrade rather than stop; words not numbers on the price page | Needs a cheap in-house fallback; OpenAI's funnel scale |
| Midjourney | Users plan around a visible hour count (anchoring evidence) | Relax mode rides free idle GPU; API-billed chat has no idle capacity |
| Windsurf, Kilo | Daily/weekly refreshing allowance, "most users never hit it" | Professional daily token volume |
| Claude, Perplexity, Gemini | Limits stated in words; weekly on top of session windows | Their cost per message is tiny; the window is abuse control, not cost control |
| Adobe Firefly | Unlimited cheap tier plus metered premium; enforcement after a free period reads as a trap | Creative Cloud price level |
| Meshy, Tripo, Rodin | Permanent vs expiring credits; pay on confirm (Rodin) | The output is the product and can be withheld; a chat's cost is spent before usefulness is known |
| Suno, Udio | Daily reset for bursty use; free = make and share, paid = export | A public feed where free output markets the product |
| Canva, CapCut | Cheap AI uncounted, expensive AI metered; "beta" framing | Feature-rich free product carrying the AI |
| Nabu Casa | One flat price, one bundle, "funds development" on the price page, "works fully without it" | Fixed infrastructure cost, not per-use inference |
| Zed, Cline, Ollama | Free BYOK path kept complete; hosted inference at cost or thin markup; small included credit | Heavy daily usage that made flat fees lose money |
| MakerWorld, Printables, Thangs | This audience pays creators, not platforms, and expects free access | Nothing to licence in an AI slicer feature |
| Strava, onX, Planta | Annual as default with a large discount; data stays free on lapse; warn monthly payers before a rise | Social graph or legal need keeping the free product in use |
| Stripe/Chargebee dunning, Peloton | Retries and email timing move involuntary churn measurably | Hardware lock-in |
| Brazil pricing, ChatGPT Go | A BRL-billed ~$7 tier exists at exactly this price point; Pix recurring tooling exists | Local entity and acquiring; OpenAI's brand pull |
| Midjourney ratings, Tesla, Common Voice | Pairwise rating with the artefact on screen reaches volume; goals lift return rate modestly; a gated access score (Tesla) was gamed | No evidence found either way on whether rewarded rating data was useful or gamed; sensors capture the outcome; Obico's own rewarded labelling is the better evidence for this audience |
| Duolingo, Cursor Tab | Behaviour is the label, no rating step | Immediate, unambiguous label; a print result is hours later and off-screen |
| Perplexity Sonar, Character.ai | Adding an own model as an option drew no noise; removing old models did | Different product category |

## Struck from the original case list (no source supported them)

- Kilo Code having an in-house unlimited model.
- Midjourney rating parties rewarding Fast hours (the party page offers no reward; Fast hours come from a separate daily queue).
- A dated own-model swap at Jasper or Grammarly.
- "$8 to 20 entry plans" for 3D generation tools.
- Roo Code and Continue as live hosted-plan cases (both shut down in 2026).
- A "Prusa Club" paid tier run by Prusa (Clubs are creator-run).
- A Strava AI-feature price reaction in 2025.
- A comma.ai founding-cohort programme.

## Could not verify (official pages blocked or silent)

Current ChatGPT, Midjourney, Claude support, Perplexity pricing and Adobe FAQ pages (403/404; snippets and mirrors

# JusPrin 2 pricing: the mental model (working doc, 2026-10-29)

Untracked working document for the pricing brainstorm. Facts, hypotheses, goal and comparables, kept apart on purpose. No recommendations here. Companion data: `v1-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (JusPrin v1 production data) and `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (Obico Pro production data, same audience).

Sourcing rule for the comparables: every figure comes from a page fetched or a search result read on 2026-10-29 by a research agent. "Vendor" marks a company's own page; "3P, loosely held" marks a third-party tracker, blog or news summary. Items from the original case list that no source supported are struck and listed at the end.

## Goal (Kenneth's words)

Traction, measured as active users and time in the app. Become the default AI harness for 3D slicing. Reduce friction as long as no choice now blocks turning profitable later. Collect feedback good enough to fine-tune small models later; willing to subsidise model cost to get it. The two audiences (people who already slice in OrcaSlicer, people who cannot) are believed to overlap heavily and converge. Sign-in is not required when the person uses their own API key.

Not yet decided: the traction number and horizon.

## Hypotheses

Each is a hypothesis until the named check is done. Survey evidence is noted where it bears on one.

1. **A premium chat costs $0.20 to $0.50 for a simple case.** Kenneth's estimate. Measured 2026-10-28 on Opus 5.5 in three harness chats: $0.30, $0.43 and $0.56. **Measured 2026-10-30 on Opus 5.5, pictures on, source at `2f9d322dee` (`journey-cost-2026-10.md`), one run each:** a simple 3-turn session $0.30, which fits, but a 5-turn troubleshooting session $0.64 ($0.66 with a photo) and a 6-turn complex session $1.27 do not. These are sessions with several turns and slices, so the range holds for the simple case only. Scripted turns follow within seconds; a person who pauses over 5 minutes before every turn would pay about $0.64, $2.56 and $1.49 (calculated from the logs, not measured), because Anthropic's cache lasts 5 minutes and rewriting it is the largest cost. **Measured 2026-11-01 on Claude Sonnet 5.5, pictures on, same scripted words, source `69780c7af4` plus the harness fix `01ec46a4af` (a newer build than the Opus runs; `journey-cost-2026-10.md`, "Sonnet 5.5, added 2026-11-01"), one run each:** the same sessions cost $0.19 (simple, 3 turns), $0.34 (complex, 6 turns) and $0.35 ($0.37 with the photo, troubleshooting, 5 turns), priced at Sonnet 5.5's rates of $2 input, $0.10 cache read, $2.50 five-minute cache write and $10 output per million tokens (fetched 2026-11-01). That is 0.64, 0.26 and 0.55 (0.56 with photo) of Opus's cost, and 0.40 over all 14 user messages ($0.063 a message against Opus's $0.158 and DeepSeek's $0.024). So the assumption that a Sonnet-class expert tier costs about half of Opus holds on two sessions (0.55 to 0.64, because Sonnet used 11 to 28% more tokens than Opus on the same words) and is pessimistic on the third (0.26, because Opus's complex run paid a $0.36 cache expiry during a slow slice and Sonnet's did not). The simple Sonnet session ($0.19) is just under the $0.20 to $0.50 range; the troubleshooting and complex sessions ($0.35, $0.34) fall inside it. Caveat: the Opus and Sonnet runs used different builds, and I did not run Opus on the new one. Check: gateway token accounting on real v2 chats, including real pauses.
2. **A cheap model costs roughly 15 to 30 times less per chat.** Guess from memory. **Measured 2026-10-30, same build, DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter with pictures removed, one run each:** $0.015, $0.31 and $0.020 against Opus's $0.30, $1.27 and $0.64, so 20 times, 4 times and 33 times less. The 4 times is the complex session, where DeepSeek polled the slicer 75 times during a slow slice on a debug build; those requests were two thirds of its cost, and without them the ratio is about 12 times (calculated). Answer quality was not compared. Check: gateway accounting on a shipped build, and whether the polling can be stopped.
3. **An engaged v2 user's monthly usage is unknown, and v1's overall medians do not estimate it.** Earlier versions of this model used v1's median payer (6.5 chats per 30 days) as "typical demand" and concluded a sub-$10 all-premium plan was profitable for most payers. That was wrong: the medians describe people who had stopped using v1. Using the first paid month instead (median 17.5 chats, 90th percentile 51 per 30 days) and Kenneth's $0.35 per chat, an engaged month costs about $6 at the median and $18 at the 90th percentile, so a $7 flat all-premium plan sits at break-even for the engaged median and underwater for the engaged tail. Kenneth's expectation (confirmed 2026-10-29): an engaged v2 user will use more than v1's first paid month showed, because v1's low numbers came from people leaving. So v1's first month is a floor for engaged usage, not an estimate, and v2 starts chats on file open and runs tools, which pushes the same way. Consequence: at $0.35 a chat an engaged user costs more than $6 a month on a frontier model, so a sub-$10 all-premium flat plan is underwater for engaged people from the start, and the cheap model or a budget is a launch question, not a later one. With the 2026-10-30 session measurements (Opus 5.5 $0.30 for a simple session, $0.64 for troubleshooting, $1.27 for a complex one, before real pauses), the same floor month costs $5 to $22 at the median of 17.5 sessions and $15 to $65 at the 90th percentile of 51, depending on the mix; on DeepSeek V4 Flash the same months cost $0.26 to $5.40 and $0.77 to $16, with the complex-session figure inflated by slice polling on a debug build. Check: beta cohort on the live gateway, measured on people still active in month two.
4. **The cheap model is good enough for the basic job.** Untested on the real task. Check: prompt eval harness vs Sonnet on print-setup cases, with image handling, at approved spend.
5. **A visible cap becomes a break-even anchor.** Supported in part: Midjourney users plan their month around hours. Refined by the survey: the anger spike in every case is at the boundary (silent swaps, meters disagreeing with cutoffs, "slower" turning into a wall), not at the number itself.
6. **A fallback keeps the session and still converts; a wall ends it.** ChatGPT and Gemini both degrade rather than stop, and the complaints are about the swap being silent. Unmeasured whether a fallback converts.
7. **Behaviour carries training signal for free, and rewarded explicit feedback from this audience is high quality.** The first half is supported by v1 (about 3,000 corrective follow-ups against 16 ratings) and by the surveyed cases that published measured gains (Duolingo, Cursor Tab). The second half comes from Obico's own rewarded print-shot labelling, which Kenneth reports produced good data. An earlier version of this hypothesis said rewards invite gaming; the survey did not support that. It found no evidence either way on Midjourney's rating data, one gamed gate at Tesla that was an access score rather than a reward for feedback, and a general warning from the Open Data Institute about leaderboards. That was one case and a caution, overstated into a pattern. Possible reasons Obico's result differs from the general worry, all untested: makers are a more conscientious population, and a small company's reward feels like a fair trade rather than something to exploit. The open question is no longer whether to reward feedback but what to ask, when, and how the reward relates to the missing label, "did the print work".
8. **The two audiences overlap and converge.** Kenneth's guess. Check: segment v1 users by whether they edit settings themselves.
9. **The July 2025 usage drop was launch decay, not the paywall.** My reading. Check: the July cohort's later behaviour.
10. **Grandfathering early payers is cheap.** True at tens of payers by arithmetic.
11. **The user base is heavily Brazilian; failed renewals are payment-method failures.** Half confirmed: v1 users are 35% US and 10% Brazil, but v1 payers are 16 of 34 Brazilian and 10 of 15 failed renewals were Brazilian cards. The payment-method mechanism is still unconfirmed: Chargebee records only "card declined" and "insufficient funds", never whether a cross-border or recurring charge was refused. Obico, 64% US payers, loses 30% of cancellations to failed payments too, so part of v1's rate is ordinary.
19. **New from Obico: a trial end converts more reliably than a usage cap.** Obico's lifetime conversion is 5%, and nearly half of its payers paid within the automatic trial window; v1 converted 0.7%, at a cap that 1% of months reach. Untested whether a trial works here: v1's median first week was 2.5 chats, but that median includes the 41% who never came back, so an engaged person's first week is unknown and almost certainly busier.
20. **New from Obico: the leading stated reason for cancelling is not using the product, far ahead of price.** This fits v1's silent later months. It is a hypothesis that a plan costing nothing in idle months (prepaid, usage-based, or annual priced for insurance) retains better than monthly; Obico's 77% annual renewal despite half-silent month 12 is the one data point.
21. **New from Obico: conversion in this audience fell four-fold after 2022 for unknown reasons**, while signups grew. Whatever caused it may bear on JusPrin's funnel too; nothing here tests the printer-camera explanation.
12. **New from the survey: "unlimited" survives only where marginal cost is near zero** (idle GPU queue, tab completions, own small models). No surveyed vendor offers unlimited frontier chat. For JusPrin this holds until the own-model phase.
13. **New: flat-fee hosted inference on rented frontier models gets repriced within about a year** (Zed) or the business leaves (Roo, Continue). Observed in daily-use professional tools with high token volume; a hobbyist slicer's volume is far lower, so the dynamic may not apply at the same scale.
14. **New: free tiers in costly-generation tools gate the artefact, not the generation** (download, export, commercial rights). A slicer chat has no equivalent artefact; the question is whether anything in JusPrin plays that role.
15. **New: a daily reset fits bursty hobby use better than a monthly one** (Suno). Untested here; v1 bursts are multi-day project sessions, not single days.
16. **New: "beta" or "trial" wording on a free allowance keeps the option to change it** (CapCut, Adobe's unenforced credits). Adobe shows the cost: the later enforcement was read as a bait and switch.
17. **New: seasonal hobby apps make annual the default and keep the person's own data free on lapse** (Strava, onX). v1's annual payers used about 33 chats a year against $59.99, a churn-shaped average (most of those years went quiet after the first month), not what an engaged year looks like.
18. **New: a quarter to half of failed renewals are recoverable by retries and email timing** (vendor figures). v1's 14 of 23 is too small a sample for a rate.

## Questions the survey raises for JusPrin (not answers)

1. Every surveyed vendor states limits in words and hides the number. Is there a reason JusPrin's price page should show a number at all, given v1's usage shape?
2. The anger is at the boundary. What exactly does the person see at JusPrin's boundary: a notice, a model change, a slower answer, a wall? Which of these fits "time in the app" as the metric?
3. "Unlimited" survives only at near-zero marginal cost. Does the word belong anywhere in JusPrin's plan before the own-model phase, and if it does, what fair-use mechanism backs it?
4. Costly-generation tools gate the artefact. Is there an artefact in JusPrin (saved project history, export, print report) that could play that role, or is the chat itself the only thing to meter?
5. Suno resets daily; v1 bursts span several days. Would a per-session or weekly allowance match project sessions better than either daily or monthly?
6. Nabu Casa prints "funds development" as a benefit and users say they pay for it. JusPrin is open source with a complete BYOK path. Does the hosted plan carry a support-the-project framing, and does that fit a Brazilian-heavy hobbyist base?
7. Zed lost money per paying customer on flat-fee frontier inference. At v1's engaged-month volume (median 17.5 chats, 90th percentile 51) and $0.35 a chat, a $7 flat plan is at break-even for the median engaged payer and underwater for the tail, before payment fees. At what chats-per-payer does the plan break, with the measured v2 cost, and does that argue for the cheap model from day one rather than later?
8. ChatGPT Go in Brazil is R$39.99, billed in BRL. Would a BRL price with recurring Pix change v1's failed-renewal pattern more than any plan-structure change? Stripe offers Pix Automático to US merchants with USD settlement, so the question is the 3.5% IOF line, the 3-day pre-debit notice and the Ebanx name on the statement, not a legal entity.
9. Obico's rewarded print-shot labels came back high quality, and v1's correction signal sits in follow-up messages for free. If the one missing label is "did the print work", what is the lowest-friction way to ask it once per print, what reward matches it (expert chats, detection hours, something else), and how does the reward avoid becoming a visible count that anchors the plan's value?
10. Perplexity added its own model as an option and nobody complained. When JusPrin's fine-tuned model arrives, is it an option beside the frontier model, or a replacement?
11. Obico converts at the end of an automatic trial; v1 converted at a cap that 1% of months reach. Which moment fits JusPrin, where the engaged first week is unknown (v1's median of 2.5 chats is churn-shaped), and does a chat-counted trial (first N expert chats) end earlier or later than a time trial for an engaged person?
12. Obico's top cancel reason is "not using it", and its annual plan renews at 77% while half of month-12 subscribers are idle. Is JusPrin's paid plan insurance in the same way, or is a chat too deliberate an act for people to keep paying for the quiet months?
13. Obico payers are mostly US; v1 payers were mostly Brazilian, with the same $6.99 price. Is that the product, the marketing channel, or the price's purchasing power? Which audience is v2 built and marketed for?
14. Obico's conversion fell four-fold after 2022 with signups growing. Does the same force act on JusPrin's funnel, and does v2 pricing need to assume a low-conversion world?

## Still missing before deciding

- Whether v1's Brazilian failed renewals were cross-border refusals or real insufficient funds (Chargebee cannot say; a BRL/Pix test cohort could).
- Why Obico's conversion fell after 2022.
- Measured v2 cost per chat and calls per chat from the gateway.
- v2 chats per person from a beta cohort.
- Cheap-model quality on the real task.
- Kenneth's traction number and horizon.

The document has one section titled "Goal (Kenneth's words)" and no section labeled priorities. Here is what it lists.

**Goals, as the doc states them (section at line 7 of [pricing-mental-model-2026-10.md](pricing-mental-model-2026-10.md:7)):**

- **Traction** is the goal, measured as active users and time in the app.
- **Become the default AI harness for 3D slicing.**
- **Reduce friction**, as long as no choice made now blocks turning profitable later.
- **Collect feedback good enough to fine-tune small models later.** The doc says you are willing to subsidise model cost to get that feedback.
- **Audience assumption:** the two audiences, people who already slice in OrcaSlicer and people who cannot, are believed to overlap heavily and converge.
- **Sign-in is not required** when the person uses their own API key.
- **Not yet decided:** the traction number and the time horizon.

**On priorities:** the doc does not rank anything explicitly. The ordering it implies is traction first, with friction reduction and feedback collection subordinate to it, and profitability treated as a constraint on today's choices rather than a goal for now. That ranking is my reading of the wording, not something the doc states.

The rest of the file is deliberately kept apart from the goal: a Facts section (v1 and Obico Pro production data, current system, other businesses), 21 numbered Hypotheses with the check each needs, a Comparables table, 14 open Questions the pricing survey raises, and a "Still missing before deciding" list. ([[figma-jusprin-v2-file]]). Since 2026-10-20 these artifacts ARE the source of truth ([[design-source-is-claude-artifacts]]); edit them directly. The Figma re-sync steps below are history.

1. Design System: https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL (version 9)
   - `tokens.json` + `tokens.css`, 37 coded React components (`window.JusPrin`).
   - Each component card: every variant Figma draws, a Light and a Dark panel,

   - `screens/<page>/<screen>.spec.txt` (166) + `screens/index.json`: plain

2. Design canvas "JusPrin v2": https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v
   (version 7): 10 pages with Figma's names in Figma's order, 198 artboards at
   their Figma x,y and in Figma's layer order, each drawn in the Light or Dark
   mode Figma sets on it; "… · Light & Dark" review frames are drawn whole.

Tools, reads and backups are durable now, outside the repo:
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/` — start with
its `README.md` (step-by-step re-sync). `published/` is an exact copy of what is

scripts that reproduce it byte for byte.

How Kenneth wants a re-sync done (2026-10-13): back up first, re-import, then
compare the backup with the new import so nothing already in sync regresses.
The method that worked, in order:
- rebuild from the old reads and require byte-identical output (proves the
  scripts);
- re-read Figma with the old script and diff the reads (proves Figma unchanged:
  all 14 files were identical);
- only then change scripts, and explain every file `compare_builds.py` reports;
- score every artboard against Figma's own page screenshots
  (`visual_compare.py`) and allow no artboard to score worse.
Result of that run: 0 artboards further from Figma, 36 closer; boards within 5
of Figma (0–255 scale) went from 99 to 122 of 186; all 37 cards and 163 of 166
spec files came out byte-identical; tokens matched Figma's variables exactly.

What the screenshot comparison caught that file checks could not: dark panels I
had added behind dark variants (Figma has none), frames forced dark by a "dark"
in their name (use Figma's `explicitVariableModes` instead), a frame half light
and half dark through a nested mode, sets whose background is a two-stop linear
gradient, Figma's GRID layout (children need their own positions), and small
frames centred in the 40px-minimum artboard instead of top-left.

Other traps: an absolutely positioned layer followed by in-flow siblings paints
over them in HTML (give the later siblings `position:relative`); Figma tints
icons with a mask plus a coloured rectangle; the Artifact tool's bulk read
prints small text files into context, so have a background agent do large
backups; a session scratchpad is wiped on restart — never keep the only copy of
tools there; when two reads of a page exist, keep the later one by timestamp.

dark status colours (Figma #4CAF82 / #E07080 / #E8B84A, code #58B894 / #F07A8E /
#E9B960), `radius/full` 10 vs `pill` 9999, Button/Icon 32px vs 26px, Menu/Row
36px full-width hover vs the app's 32px inset rows
([[header-menu-values-kenneth-kept]]). See also [[figma-mcp-view-seat-limit]]

Publishing (2026-10-20, filament step): a publish is refused as "haven't viewed the latest version" unless this session did a plain `read` of the artifact url (path reads alone do not count). # Where a person meets the credits, and how each point should feel (working doc, 2026-11-01, synced to canvas version 71; balances changed to credits only on 2026-11-02 evening, canvas update pending on 2026-11-02)

**Decided 2026-11-02 evening, after Kenneth saw canvas version 73. These override anything below that says otherwise.**
- Every credit is the same. There is no Standard-only lot. Any mention below of a `basic_only` flag, a "trickle" of Standard-only credits, "Free Standard messages" or "Free Standard credits" is superseded. free accounts (not subscribed) get 50 credits a month, expiring one month after grant, that pay for either tier; Kenneth to the design session: "the 'everyone gets 50 credits' wording is wrong. I never said that." (Kenneth: "let's just give free users 50/mo use-it-or-loose it credits").
- Workshop has no ceiling. Standard messages cost 0 credits on Workshop (Kenneth: "no ceiling. It's probably easier just to say standard messages cost 0 credits"). Anything below about 600, fair use, or a notice at 500 or 600 is superseded.
- A balance is one number of credits, never a count of messages beside it. The panel shows one bar per lot, grouped only by when the credits expire: "First-month credits · 62 of 500 left · Expires 1 Dec", "Bought credits · 500 of 500 left · Never expire". Bought credits get a bar like the others (decision 13 closed).
- "New Standard chat" and board 3d are gone: the case only existed because a Standard-only lot could not pay for an Expert chat. A chat that cannot be paid offers "Get more credits" only.
- Prices in messages appear only on the picker options, the stop card for the chat's own tier, the pricing page's one sentence, the low-balance notice, and one scale line under the first-month offer ("An Expert message is 5 credits").
- Kenneth reviewed the list of mechanisms that were mine, not his (2026-11-02, late evening). **Kept:** the launch offer (double credits on packs until a date); the low-balance notice, reworded to "About 25 credits left" (credits, not messages); "Expiring credits are used first" in the panel; the "Alert me when a subscription would save me money" switch, on by default; the Account page shape (30-day total, bar chart per day, table of chats); Standard as the default tier for a new chat after the first month; the v1 welcome-back fill-ins; the print-report form details; alias ids `slicer-1` and `slicer-basic` with image stripping. **Dropped:** the reverse savings alert and board 7c; the month-end and 7-day expiry notices (rule 4 on board 0 loses them); the daily cap on free app turns; the thinking picker on Standard (Expert only). **Expiry:** every expiring lot expires one month from the day it was granted, never at a calendar month end: first-month credits a month after sign-in, the free 50 a month after each grant, plan credits with the billing cycle.
- Free credits, ruled 2026-11-02 late: "no 50 credits for first month. only 500 initial credits. pack holders also get 50 credits a month." So the 50 a month goes to every account not on a subscription, starting after the first month; a pack holder gets it; during the first month there is only the 500. The balance example on 2a, 4a and 4b is 62 first-month + 500 bought = 562, with no Free credits bar. Footer: "After your first month, accounts without a plan get 50 free credits a month."

Untracked design notes. The pricing plan is in `pricing-implementation-plan-2026-11.md`; this document is about the person, not the ledger. It lists every point in the product where someone meets credits, says what goes wrong there in other products, and gives one opinion per point. Kenneth reviewed the boards on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ) between versions 54 and 70; the boards are now the source of truth and this document follows them. Captures are in `design-captures/credits-2026-11/` (`credits-00` to `credits-09`).

Where the boards live on the canvas (decided 2026-11-02: boards sit with the flow they change, not on a feature page): the onboarding boards (1a to 1d, 6a, 6b) on "On boarding experience"; the composer states (2a to 2c, 3a to 3d, 7a to 7c) on "Compositions" beside the Composer; the Account boards (4a to 4c) on "Agent setup & Preferences"; the report boards (8a to 8d) on "Print history". "Credits & plans" keeps only what has no flow of its own: the five rules (board 0), the pricing page (5a, 5b) and the states overview (9). Every board has "Credits" in its canvas name so a search finds the set.

What the survey of other products (`pricing-case-studies-2026-10.md`) says goes wrong, in one list: people cannot picture what an abstract credit buys; two kinds of credit with different expiry rules confuse everyone; the anger is at the boundary, when something they were doing stops; a balance that drops for reasons they did not cause breeds distrust; "unlimited" with an unstated ceiling is read as a lie once reached.

## Five rules that apply at every point (board 0)

1. **One word, one unit, credits only.** "Credits" (decided 2026-11-01), never coins, never tokens. A balance is a number of credits and nothing else: "562 credits left." Kenneth, 2026-11-02: showing a count of messages beside the credits is confusing; consolidate everything into credits. (Canvas versions up to 71 and my earlier drafts put "That is 612 Standard or 112 Expert messages" under every balance; that was my addition, never his decision, and it is gone.) The translation into messages appears only where the person chooses or is stopped: the picker options, the stop card for the chat's own tier, the pricing page's one sentence, and one scale line under the first-month offer ("An Expert message is 5 credits"). The low-balance notice "About 25 credits left" stays, because there the person needs to know how many turns this chat has left. A price never stands alone: "1 credit" confused Kenneth on sight (2026-11-02), so it is always "1 credit a message", "5 credits a message". Dollars appear only on the page where money changes hands. Plans are Hobby ($10 a month), Workshop ($20 a month) and Pay as you go (the never-expiring pack); never Pro, Plus or Premium.
2. **Credits only move when the person sends a message.** Turns the app starts (the file-opened report, the slice-finished note) are free, and the balance never changes without a message from the person. That one fact is what makes the balance trustworthy; it is stated on the pricing page in one sentence: "Only messages you send cost credits."
3. **Expiring credits are named by what they are, with a date. Bought credits are just "credits" and never expire.** "First-month credits · 62 of 500 left · Expires 1 Dec." "Free Standard credits · 50 of 50 left · Resets 1 Dec · Standard only." "Bought credits · 500 left · Never expire." Never a bare number that mixes them. The draw rule is stated once, in the breakdown: "Expiring credits are used first."
4. **Say the number before the boundary, not at it.** Every ceiling (balance, fair use, expiry) is shown on the way there with a count, so reaching it is never news.
5. **Nothing typed is lost and nothing stops silently.** A message that cannot be sent stays in the composer. (The earlier draft added "with a way to send it anyway"; the design session dropped the phrase on board 0 because a chat now keeps its model, so there is no way to send. That follows from Kenneth's decision but he has not reviewed the wording. The ways forward are to get more credits or, when free Standard messages remain, to start a Standard chat with the typed text carried over.)

## Decisions from the review that shape several points

- **The cheap tier is "Standard".** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, in the brainstorm session: not "Basic" (the first boards' word, which sells the tier on being the lesser one) and not "Quick" (my suggestion). Every surface uses it: "Standard · 1 credit a message", "Unlimited Standard messages", "Free Standard credits", "50 free Standard credits this month", "New Standard chat", and rule 1's explanation. Canvas version 71 says Standard on every board.

- **A chat keeps its model.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, board 3b: for now a person cannot switch the model mid-chat. The model and thinking pickers stay in the composer once a chat has a message, greyed, and hovering either shows a two-line tooltip: "A chat keeps the model and thinking level it started with. Start a new chat to change them." and "Each message you send in this chat costs 5 credits." (board 2c). So there is no "Send with Standard" and no "Switch this chat to Standard" anywhere.
- **The app's own turns run on Expert, cost nothing, and do not fix the chat's model.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, brainstorm session. The turn the app starts when a file opens has to read the plate picture, so it runs on Expert whatever the person would pick; it is free under rule 2; and it does not count as the chat's first message. The person's first message fixes the chat's model, and the greyed pickers follow that message, not the app's note. Without this, every chat that begins with a file would be pinned to Expert before the person could choose, since today the app's note takes the account default and fixes the chat to it.
- **A picture in a Standard chat is dropped, and the attachment row says so.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, brainstorm session: the Standard model cannot see pictures, and he rejected a long clause in the picker option. The notice lives on the staged attachment itself (point 2).
- **One action outside the pricing page: "Get more credits".** Kenneth, board 3c: at the moment someone runs out they cannot judge a pack against a plan from a button label, so there is no "Buy" beside "Subscribe" in the app. "Get more credits" opens the pricing page, which explains the difference. The one exception is the savings alert (point 7), whose "Subscribe" names one plan and shows the sums.

## The points, in the order a person meets them

### 1. First launch: own key or JusPrin account (boards 1a to 1d)

Where: the Agent setup in Preferences › Agent (the one setup flow, decided 2026-10-23) and the welcome screen.

Kenneth's reaction to the first draft, which put the offer as a small line under "Set up JusPrin": "the most non-obvious way to urge user to sign up". Opinion, as drawn: the offer is the headline on its own surface, "Your first month: 500 credits", with the translation under it, "An Expert message is 5 credits. Your own API key stays free.", and the button names the reward, "Sign in for 500 credits". "Explore first" moves below it. Never "trial" (decided): a trial promises a wall at the end. No dollar figure. The same hierarchy is on the setup row (1a), the welcome screen (1b) and the welcome-back window for a returning v1 user (1c), where signing in is the primary button and Continue secondary. It is "Your own API key", not "your own key" (Kenneth, board 1a).

v1 subscribers (Kenneth, board 1c: "make it clear that JusPrin v1 subscribers grandfathered to the $10/mo tier with the original price", "in addition to getting 500 credits"). 1c adds the line "Subscribed to JusPrin v1? You get these 500 credits and keep your original price, on the $10 Hobby plan.", conditional because the app cannot know until sign-in. Board 1d is what that person sees once signed in: "Hobby, at your original $6.99 a month. 750 credits a month. Plus 500 more for your first month. New subscribers pay $10. You keep this price while subscribed." Nothing to choose, no upgrade prompt; the annual plan reads "at your original $59.99 a year". The design session's fill-ins, not yet confirmed: the price holds "while subscribed"; the 500 stack on the 750 in the first month; and when the move happens (at sign-in or at term end) and how to say that v1 was "unlimited" and Hobby is not are open. v1 has 20 active subscriptions, 15 annual and 5 monthly.

### 2. Picking Standard or Expert for a chat (boards 2b, 2c)

Where: the model picker in the composer (`ModelPickers.tsx`), chosen before the first message of a chat.

Opinion: each option gets the price with its unit and one plain clause about when to use it: "Standard · 1 credit a message · setting up an ordinary print" and "Expert · 5 credits a message · troubleshooting, tricky models, anything you'd ask a person". No model names, no vendor names: the person is choosing how much help to buy, not which company's model. On Standard the price reads "free this month" while free Standard messages last. On the person's own API key there is no price line. After the first message both pickers stay where they are, greyed, with the tooltip from the decision above. The option stays this short: no clause about pictures (Kenneth, 2026-11-02).

A picture in a Standard chat (decided 2026-11-02, board 3e on the Compositions page, capture `credits-03e-picture-in-standard-chat.png`): the composer's attachment chip already has a thumbnail, a name line, a second line and a Remove button. In a Standard chat a staged picture keeps its thumbnail, its second line reads "Standard can't see pictures, so this one will not be sent.", and the row gets a "New Expert chat" button beside Remove that starts an Expert chat carrying the typed text and the attachment, the same shape as board 3d's new-chat button. Send stays enabled and the picture is simply left out of the request. One row covers the + menu, drag-and-drop and paste, so the + menu needs no change. As drawn, the two buttons sit on their own line under the sentence, and the sentence is in primary ink rather than grey, since it is a notice and not metadata; it is not in the error colour because Send still works. A Standard chat also lists no picture-returning tools to the model (`view_render` and friends), so the model never calls a tool whose result it cannot read.

The turn the app starts when a file opens runs on Expert, free, and leaves the pickers live for the person's first message (decision above). So a chat can hold one Expert turn, the app's, followed by Standard ones; the gateway drops the pictures from that history for the Standard model.

Default for a new chat: Expert while the first-month credits last, because the first weeks decide whether the person stays. After that, Standard (board 6a). Whether a later new chat takes the last chosen tier instead is still open. Thinking levels (Fast, Thorough) are drawn at one price per tier; Expert defaults to Thorough and Standard to Fast (the design session's fill-in). Whether Standard shows a thinking picker at all is open; the brainstorm session suggested showing it only on Expert, since Standard has one price anyway.

### 3. The balance (boards 2a, 4a to 4c)

Where: the composer, and Preferences › Account.

import re,html,glob,os
from html.parser import HTMLParser
class P(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(s):
        super().__init__(); s.out=[]; s.skip=0; s.depth=0
    def handle_starttag(s,tag,attrs):
        a=dict(attrs)
        if tag in ('script','style','svg','helmet'): s.skip+=1
        if s.skip: return
        n=a.get('data-n') or a.get('data-c')
        if n and tag=='div' and ('Application header' in n or 'footer' in n or n.startswith('Button') or n.startswith('Status') or n.startswith('Icon') or n.startswith('Field')):
            pass
        if n and not n.startswith(('Icon','Status Dot')):
            s.out.append(f"\n[{n}] ")
        if tag=='br': s.out.append(' / ')
    def handle_endtag(s,tag):
        if tag in ('script','style','svg','helmet'): s.skip-=1
    def handle_data(s,d):
        if s.skip: return
        d=' '.join(d.split())
        if d: s.out.append(d+' | ')

input.recap: I read all 34 boards on the canvas's "On boarding experience" page plus the first-launch credits captures and critiqued them against the pricing doc's goals: traction, default AI harness, low friction, feedback collection. The critique is in the message. Nothing was changed on the canvas or in the repo.

content.text:
Your message cut off at "serving the". I read it as "serving the goals in the pricing doc": traction measured as active users and time in the app, becoming the default AI harness for slicing, low friction, and collecting feedback worth training on. I critiqued the 34 boards on the canvas page "On boarding experience" (onboarding 00 to 20, the three v1 welcome-back boards, and credits 1a to 1d, 6a, 6b) against those four goals.

**The core problem: the flow asks for commitment before it shows value.** A new person walks through welcome, sign-in, a code or browser round trip, an agent check, an Orca import, a physical-setup confirmation and a project choice before the agent does anything. That is seven to nine screens. The one "wow" the product has, the agent proposing a plan on the person's own model, sits at board 13. v1's data says 41% of people ever had exactly one chat. A wizard this long spends the first session on setup, which is the opposite of the "time in the app" metric.

**Where it falls short, by goal**

- **Sign-in is the first door, which contradicts the doc's own rule.** Board 00 says "Start with account setup. Connect an Agent afterward", and its footer says "Account setup comes first if you want to connect one." The doc says sign-in is not required with your own API key, and board 1b even says "Your own API key stays free", but no board offers a key path. A BYOK person must sign in or go agentless. Boards 01 to 08 also duplicate a sign-in flow that the 2026-10-23 decision moved into Preferences › Agent. The handoff doc already says those links go away. These boards are stale against that decision.
- **The sign-in ask is at the wrong moment.** The highest-intent moment is board 12, where the person types what matters for their print. Asking there ("Sign in for 500 credits to send this", message kept per rule 5) converts a person who already wants something. Asking on board 00 converts a person who has seen a static "EXAMPLE INTERACTION · NOT LIVE" box. Obico's data in the pricing doc points the same way: people convert when they want the next thing, not at the front door.
- **"Explore first" leads to a dead end for the harness goal.** The local path ends at board 19, where the agent pane is a "Set up Agent" placeholder. A person who explores never meets the agent on their own project, so the product never makes its case to the audience most likely to become engaged users, the ones who already slice in Orca.
- **The guided tour runs on a phone stand, not their part.** Boards 11 to 16 walk a "representative mockup" and end with "Open my project", which asks the person to start again. v1 usage comes in project sessions. The tour should run on the file they brought, with the example only when they have none. Board 08, the first-run Home ("Drop a model or project to start"), already has the right one-step shape. The wizard competes with it.
- **Setup steps carry friction with no payoff at that moment.** Board 10 asks the person to go check the plate on their printer during onboarding. The plate matters at slice time. Board 10a hides the one agent-powered setup step, identifying the printer from a photo or the network, behind a fork after "Configure manually". Boards 09, 17 and 18 give the preset import more screens than the first chat gets.
- **The welcome speaks to one audience.** "Your Orca workflow" and "bring along your tuned presets" address the Orca user. The doc says the two audiences converge and the product should be the default harness for both. The person who cannot slice reads a screen about a tool they do not use. The job is a good print, not a workflow migration.
- **Nothing in the flow serves the feedback goal.** No step tells the person their chats are kept, no step learns whether they edit settings themselves (the check the doc names for hypothesis 8), and nothing sets up the one label the doc calls missing, "did the print work". The flow could at least say a report will be asked for after a print.
- **Vocabulary drifts across screens.** Account, Agent, AI access, "JusPrin AI service" and "Agent connected" are five names for one thing within ten boards. "Agent" is never explained to a first-time person, and every local screen's header carries "Local mode · Agent not configured", which frames the local path as deficient.
- **The v1 subscriber boards leave a boundary surprise.** Board 1d moves the 20 most engaged people from unlimited to 750 credits a month and does not say so. The touchpoints doc flags this as open. Under the doc's own rule, say the number before the boundary, this is the place.

**What already serves the goals.** Every error state (03, 05, 07, 19a) keeps the person working with "Continue locally" and never strands them. The first-month offer on 1a to 1d is the headline and the button names the reward. Board 6a ends the first month with no wall and no modal. The v1 welcome-back path replaces boards 01 to 09 for returning people rather than making them repeat setup.

**Recommendation in one line.** Collapse the wizard to the first-run Home: open their file, let the agent's free file-opened turn show something real, and make the sign-in or key ask at the first message, with the import and physical setup deferred to the moments that need them.

The problem is the core value proposition is agent-assisted slicing. The shortest path to having an agent up and running I can think of was to ask the agent to the user to sign up first to get the 500 initial credits. What options do we have for us to show the value with a much shorter path?

The constraint is real: the agent cannot say anything until a model answers, and a model needs either a key or an account. But "account first" is only one way to meet it. The question is who pays for the first few turns and when the ask happens. Five options, cheapest to build first.

**1. Move the ask from the front door to the composer, nothing else changes.** First-run Home opens the person's file as today. The chat panel shows the agent is there, with the first-month offer inline: "Sign in for 500 credits and I'll plan this print." The sign-in is one click to Google and back, no wizard around it, and the person lands in the same chat with their file already open. The person sees their own model on the plate and the agent waiting, instead of a welcome screen with a fake example. Value shown: the product, not the agent. Cost: zero model spend. Build: small, mostly removing boards 00 to 08.

**2. Let the app's own first turn run before sign-in.** The gateway already treats app-started turns (the file-opened report) as free. Issue an anonymous device token on first launch and let that one turn run on it. The person opens a file and, within seconds, the agent describes what it sees on the plate and what it would check, then the composer asks for sign-in to continue, with the typed message kept. Value shown: a real Expert read of their actual part. Cost per install: roughly the price of one Expert turn with a plate picture. From the doc's measurements that is on the order of $0.10 to $0.30, calculated, not measured. Build: gateway token issuance, one free turn per token, rate limit per device and IP.

**3. Anonymous starter credits.** Same device token, but it carries a small lot, say enough for two or three person-sent Expert messages. Signing in converts to the 500. The person gets a plan, applies it, maybe slices, and is stopped only at the third or fourth message. By then they have something to lose, which is where Obico's conversion happens in the pricing doc. Cost per install: calculated from the doc's figures, about $0.30 to $0.80 on Opus or $0.15 to $0.35 on Sonnet. Risk: reinstall farming and use of the endpoint as a free model proxy. Both are weak attacks here, because the gateway fixes the system prompt and tools to slicing, and a device plus IP cap holds the spend to under a dollar per abuser. Build: option 2 plus a ledger entry type for anonymous lots.

**4. Own API key as an equal door at the same gate.** The doc says sign-in is not required with a key, but no board offers one. At the composer gate, "Paste an API key" beside "Sign in for 500 credits" makes the Orca power user's path one field, and that person is the loudest early adopter. Cost: zero. Build: the Preferences › Agent key row already exists, so this is a link to it from the gate.

**5. A cheap model for anonymous turns, Expert after sign-in.** Cuts option 3's cost by 10 to 20 times, from the doc's DeepSeek measurements. I would not do it: the first impression is the one impression, and hypothesis 4 (the cheap model is good enough) is untested on the real task. A weak first answer costs more users than it saves dollars.

**My pick: 1 + 2 + 4 now, 3 once 2 is measured.** Option 1 removes the wizard and costs nothing. Option 2 makes the agent's first words about the person's own part before any ask, at a cost of one turn per install, which is the kind of subsidy the doc says you are willing to pay. Option 4 honours the rule you already set. Option 3 is the same mechanism with a bigger number, so turn it on after you see how many people who got the free turn then sign in. None of these blocks profitability later: the anonymous allowance is a number you can set to zero.

One thing to decide alongside: whether the free app turn runs with the plate picture. With it, the first message is specific to their part and worth the spend. Without it, the agent can only talk about settings, which reads like any chatbot.
So we dropped the user directly onto home. And then let user open the model their own model. And then let them try it for a few messages? Is that how you imagine the first time user experiences?

Yes, that is the shape, with one correction and one gap worth naming.

**The correction: it is not "try it for a few messages" by default.** With the version I would ship first, the person gets exactly one free turn before the ask, and it is the turn the app starts, not one they type. The few-messages version is the follow-up once you have seen how many people who got that one turn then sign in.

**How I imagine the first run, step by step**

1. **Launch lands on Home, first-run state.** Empty projects, the line "Drop a model or project to start", an empty printers column. The first-month offer sits on Home as a card, headline and "Sign in for 500 credits" button, visible but not blocking. If an OrcaSlicer configuration is on the machine, one quiet row offers to import the presets in a click. No wizard.
2. **The person drops their own model.** Prepare opens with the part on the plate and the chat panel open. Someone with no file handy gets the bundled example from the same empty state.
3. **The agent speaks first, on their part, before any ask.** This is the free app-started turn, running on an anonymous device token. It describes what it sees on the plate and what it would do, and asks what the part is for. This is the moment the product makes its case, and it costs one turn per install.
4. **The person types their first message. Send is the gate.** The composer says "Sign in for 500 credits to send this" with "Paste an API key" beside it. Their text stays in the box. Sign-in is one click to the browser and back, into the same chat.
5. **From there it is the ordinary flow.** The agent proposes, the person applies, slices, checks the print, then prints or exports. Printer connection, calibration and the rest come up when the work needs them.

**The gap: the printer.** Today the workspace tools need a printer selected before the agent can do anything, and the wizard's boards 09 and 10 existed to get one chosen first. Two ways to close it, and I lean to the second:

- Home asks for the printer before the file opens, one picker, the add-printer form you already have.
- The agent's first turn handles it. If no printer is selected, its first words are "Which printer will this print on?" and the printer-setup tool does the rest, by model name, photo or the network. The wizard step becomes a conversation, which is the product's whole point. This needs a check in the code that the file-opened turn can run with no printer selected. I have not verified that.

**What the person with a file feels.** They launched, dropped their part, and within a minute an agent talked about that part specifically and asked a sensible question. Then they were asked to sign in to answer it. That is the order the pricing doc argues for: value, then the ask at the boundary, with nothing typed lost.
